segments.caption: House prices in a city: most are moderate, but a few are very expensive.
Plot them, and the shape leans to the left, with a long tail to the right.
But change the scale, and they form a perfect bell.
That's the log-normal distribution.
Here's the definition, in simple words.
A log-normal distribution has only positive values, and it's skewed to the right.
But take the log of every value, and you get a normal bell curve.
That's the name: its logs are normal.
So what's a log? Here's the easy way to think about it.
A log counts the zeros. The log of 10 is 1. The log of 100 is 2. The log of 1,000 is 3.
So on a log scale, each step means times ten.
Here are 100 house prices, in lakhs of rupees.
On a normal scale, most are bunched on the left, and a few stretch far to the right.
Now switch to a log scale.
The same prices form a symmetric bell. That's log-normal.
Why does this happen? Because prices grow by percentages.
A 10% rise adds 2 lakh to a 20 lakh flat, but 20 lakh to a 2 crore villa.
Growth that multiplies, instead of adding, stretches the big values out. That makes the long tail.
You'll see log-normal data everywhere: incomes, house prices, the time to finish a task, and stock prices.
Data science tip: when your data looks like this, take the log. Many models work better on a bell shape.
So remember: log-normal values are positive, and skewed to the right.
Take their logs, and you get a normal bell.
Quick quiz!
A dataset makes a perfect bell on a log scale.
What shape does it have on a normal scale?
Skewed to the right!
A bell on a log scale means log-normal: bunched on the left, with a long tail to the right.
